questions.text: Which is the first step in insurance planning?
questions.explanation: Insurance planning starts with identifying the risks and protection needs to be covered.

questions.text: The King’s employees’ example demonstrates insurance for:
options: Loss of income due to death
questions.explanation: It represents insurance against loss of income due to the death of an earning member.

questions.text: According to the 2015 amendment, a beneficial nominee in life insurance is:
options: Always the executor of the will
Legally entitled to the claim amount ahead of legal heirs
questions.explanation: Under Section 39(7) of the Insurance Act, a beneficial nominee (spouse, parents, or children) is entitled to receive proceeds fully.

questions.text: Which of the following diseases are now mandatorily covered under health insurance?
questions.explanation: Recent IRDAI regulations mandate inclusion of mental illnesses and genetic disorders in health insurance coverage.

questions.text: The main purpose of reviewing insurance coverage periodically is to:
options: Ensure coverage remains adequate as life circumstances change
Get a refund of past premiums
questions.explanation: Reviewing coverage ensures the insured’s protection aligns with changing income, assets, and family needs.

questions.text: As per IRDAI, for life insurance terms exceeding 10 years, the minimum sum assured must be:
options: 7 times for those above 45 years and 10 times for those below 45 years
questions.explanation: IRDAI mandates 10x of annual premium below age 45, and 7x above 45 for terms over 10 years.

questions.text: Life insurance primarily provides protection against:
options: Loss of income due to death
questions.explanation: Life insurance protects dependents from loss of income due to the death of the insured.

questions.text: If a policyholder pays higher premium to get maturity value, the implied investment return can be found using:
options: Rate or XIRR function in Excel
questions.explanation: The internal rate of return on extra premium can be calculated using RATE or XIRR functions in Excel.

questions.text: Mortgage insurance sum assured:
options: Has no relation to the loan
questions.explanation: Mortgage insurance is designed with reducing sum assured, matching the declining loan balance.

questions.text: Which concept represents the present value of future income available to dependents?
questions.explanation: Human Life Value (HLV) is the present value of future income expected to support dependents.

questions.text: Liability insurance primarily covers:
options: Loss of or damage to own assets
Legal liability to third parties for injury or property damage
questions.explanation: Liability insurance indemnifies the insured for damages payable under law to third parties.

questions.text: Directors & Officers (D&O) liability insurance covers:
options: Personal liability of directors and officers for wrongful acts in their managerial role
Only losses due to fire at office
questions.explanation: D&O policies cover legal defence costs and damages for claims alleging wrongful acts by directors/officers.

questions.text: Having multiple indemnity health policies usually:
options: Allows unlimited claims from all insurers for the same expense
Does not increase total claim beyond actual expenses
questions.explanation: Indemnity policies cannot pay more than actual loss; multiple policies only complicate claims.

questions.text: Property insurance usually covers:
options: Natural and man-made disasters like fire and theft
questions.explanation: Property insurance covers specified perils like fire, flood, and theft, not normal wear and tear or speculative losses.

questions.text: Non-life insurance primarily protects an individual against:
options: Loss or damage to assets and unexpected large expenses
questions.explanation: Non-life insurance covers loss or damage to assets and large, unexpected expenses that can drain income.

questions.text: Sequence of returns risk refers to:
options: Order of returns affecting long-term corpus sustainability
Order of fund selection by investor
questions.explanation: Negative returns early in retirement can damage sustainability even if average returns remain similar.

questions.text: The key to reducing reinvestment risk is to:
options: Use a laddering strategy across maturities
questions.explanation: Laddering investments over different maturities helps smoothen reinvestment rate fluctuations.

questions.text: Which statement about longer accumulation periods is MOST appropriate?
options: They increase the annual savings required
They reduce the compounding benefit on savings
They allow lower annual savings due to compounding
They have no impact on the savings required
questions.explanation: More years before retirement allow compounding to work longer, so required annual savings can be lower for the same goal.

questions.text: Retirement expenses are generally NOT the same as pre-retirement expenses because:
options: Some expenses fall while others like medical and leisure may rise
Housing costs always disappear at retirement
questions.explanation: Loan EMIs, work-related costs may fall, but medical, travel and recreation often rise; tax may change as income changes.

questions.text: An annuity product can help retirees by:
options: Providing guaranteed regular income for life
questions.explanation: Annuities convert corpus into guaranteed income, reducing longevity and reinvestment risk.

questions.text: Reverse mortgage is relevant in retirement planning because:
options: It allows earning from idle residential property without sale
questions.explanation: Reverse mortgage enables senior citizens to get periodic income from their home while retaining ownership.

questions.text: At maturity, a minimum of what percentage of NPS corpus must be used to buy an annuity?
questions.explanation: 40% of the NPS corpus must be used to purchase an annuity at retirement.

questions.text: To reduce reinvestment risk in debt products, retirees can use:
questions.explanation: Bond or FD laddering helps manage reinvestment risk by staggering maturities.

questions.text: Liquidity in a retirement portfolio is essential to handle:
questions.explanation: Liquidity helps meet unexpected expenses without disturbing income assets.

questions.text: The tenure of PMVVY is:
questions.explanation: PMVVY offers guaranteed income for 10 years.

questions.text: Voluntary Provident Fund (VPF) refers to:
options: Employee’s voluntary contribution beyond the mandatory 12%
questions.explanation: Employees can contribute more than the statutory 12% as VPF; it earns the same interest as EPF.

questions.text: Maximum investment under POMIS for single account holder is:
questions.explanation: The maximum investment permitted under POMIS is ₹15 lakh.

questions.text: Before making retirement recommendations, an adviser should first understand:
options: Client’s horoscope and place of birth
Expected time horizon, income needs, assets and liabilities
questions.explanation: Sound advice requires assessing time horizon, income needs, assets, liabilities, and client’s overall risk appetite.

questions.text: When evaluating retirement products, which factor reduces real long-term gains the most?
questions.explanation: Tax inefficiency erodes long-term real returns, so tax treatment is a key selection criterion.

questions.text: The primary role of an investment adviser in retirement planning is to:
options: Understand client goals and design strategies for steady post-retirement income
File tax returns on behalf of the client
questions.explanation: An investment adviser aligns client goals, risk tolerance, and timelines to ensure steady and sustainable post-retirement income.

questions.text: In the pre-retirement phase, the focus should be on products that:
options: Generate fixed income with low growth
Allow growth through market participation despite some risk
questions.explanation: During accumulation, higher risk tolerance allows for equity or market-linked growth products.

questions.text: A key responsibility of an adviser while planning retirement income is to decide:
options: Client’s asset allocation and withdrawal rate
questions.explanation: Advisers determine sustainable withdrawal rates and design asset allocation to support income longevity.

questions.text: A good way for advisers to initiate discussion on philanthropy is to:
options: Link the conversation to life events or financial milestones
questions.explanation: Major life or liquidity events create natural opportunities to discuss charitable giving.

questions.text: Which deduction is available for investment in NPS (self-contribution)?
questions.explanation: Section 80CCD(1B) provides additional deduction up to ₹50,000 for NPS contribution by an individual.

questions.text: Unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward for how many years?
questions.explanation: Unabsorbed depreciation can be carried forward indefinitely until fully set off.

questions.text: Long-term capital gains under the new regime are taxed at:
questions.explanation: Under the new provisions applicable from 23 July 2024, long-term capital gains are taxed at 12.5%.

questions.text: Under Section 54F, exemption is available when the net consideration is reinvested in:
questions.explanation: Section 54F provides exemption if net sale consideration from any long-term capital asset is invested in a residential house.

questions.text: Winnings from lotteries and online games are taxable at a flat rate of:
questions.explanation: Section 115BB taxes winnings from lotteries, crossword puzzles, and online games at 30% plus applicable surcharge and cess.

questions.text: No deduction is allowed against which income under 'Other Sources'?
questions.explanation: No deduction or allowance is permitted for winnings from lotteries, crossword puzzles, or online games.

questions.text: Which type of mutual fund invests primarily in government and corporate debt?
questions.explanation: Debt mutual funds invest mainly in fixed-income instruments like government bonds and corporate debt.

questions.text: As per Finance Act 2024, unlisted bonds and market-linked debentures are always treated as:
questions.explanation: Unlisted bonds and MLDs are always taxed as short-term capital assets, regardless of holding period.

questions.text: Equity-oriented mutual funds qualify as long-term capital assets after holding for:
questions.explanation: Units of equity-oriented mutual funds are long-term if held for more than 12 months.

questions.text: Equity investments primarily generate income from:
questions.explanation: Equity investors earn through dividend distributions and capital gains when shares appreciate in value.

questions.text: Category-I and II AIFs enjoy pass-through status for which type of income?
questions.explanation: Pass-through applies to capital gains and other income, not to business income, which is taxed at AIF level.

questions.text: Before October 2024, buyback tax was paid by:
questions.explanation: Prior to October 2024, domestic companies paid 20% buyback tax, and shareholders’ income was exempt under Section 10(34A).

questions.text: The key principle of estate planning is:
questions.explanation: Estate planning ensures clarity, legal compliance, and proper intent for asset transfer.

questions.text: Estate taxes in India are:
questions.explanation: Estate duty was abolished in 1985; inheritance is currently tax-free in India.

questions.text: Under Muslim law, how much of one’s estate can be disposed of by Will?
questions.explanation: Muslim law allows disposition of up to one-third of estate by will; balance passes to legal heirs.

questions.text: What is 'Net Estate'?
options: Total value of all assets owned by an individual
Estate value after deducting debts and liabilities
questions.explanation: Net Estate is computed after deducting debts, taxes, and expenses from the gross estate value.

questions.text: Who can be a nominee under the Companies Act for shares?
options: Any person authorized in the demat account
questions.explanation: A shareholder can nominate anyone by recording nomination in the demat account.

questions.text: When a person dies without a will, it is termed as:
questions.explanation: When no will exists, the person is said to have died intestate and property distribution follows succession laws.

questions.text: Which of the following is a disadvantage of a trust?
questions.explanation: Trusts can be expensive and complex to maintain, though legally recognized.

questions.text: The Distributable Net Income (DNI) of a trust represents:
options: Income available for distribution to beneficiaries
questions.explanation: DNI denotes income available for distribution after deducting expenses and exemptions.

questions.text: Which document specifies an individual’s medical treatment preferences?
questions.explanation: A Living Will defines medical treatment choices if the person becomes incapacitated.

questions.text: Which section of Income Tax Act exempts capital gains on transfer to an irrevocable trust?
questions.explanation: Transfers under an irrevocable trust are exempt under Section 47(iii).

questions.text: What is the primary benefit of creating a trust for minor children?
options: Ensuring controlled use of funds until maturity
questions.explanation: Trusts can manage assets for minors until they reach a defined age.

questions.text: What is a Codicil?
options: A supplementary document altering a Will
questions.explanation: A codicil modifies, explains, or adds to a Will and forms part of it.

questions.text: According to Kindleberger, bubbles persist because:
options: Coordination and timing problems among rational arbitrageurs
questions.explanation: Even rational arbitrageurs face timing and coordination challenges, allowing bubbles to persist.

questions.text: Fusion Investing attempts to integrate:
questions.explanation: Fusion Investing combines insights from fundamental and behavioural finance to design strategies.

questions.text: Piotroski Score is used to:
questions.explanation: The Piotroski Score evaluates a firm’s financial strength based on nine accounting parameters.

questions.text: The primary behavioural issue behind frequent trading is:
questions.explanation: Frequent trading often arises from the action bias — the urge to 'do something' rather than stay invested.

questions.text: Chasing trends like gold or equities based on last year's returns demonstrates:
questions.explanation: Recency bias makes investors rely too much on recent performance, assuming it will persist.

questions.text: The opposite of over-diversification is:
questions.explanation: Having too few investments creates concentration risk, exposing investors to higher volatility.

questions.text: Risk profiling involves assessing which three factors?
options: Ability, Willingness, and Need to take risk
Tax rate, Portfolio value, and Tenure
questions.explanation: Risk profiling considers ability (financial capacity), willingness (psychological comfort), and need (goal requirement).

questions.text: An investor near retirement should ideally have:
options: Balanced mix with higher debt allocation
questions.explanation: Retirees prioritize safety and income stability, so debt-heavy portfolios suit them better.

questions.text: In the coin toss example, the difference in people's decisions highlights:
questions.explanation: The example illustrates how individuals differ in their risk appetite despite similar expected returns.

questions.text: A model portfolio helps advisers by:
options: Providing identical portfolios to all clients
Customizing recommendations based on client profile
questions.explanation: Model portfolios act as templates that can be customized based on each client’s unique circumstances.

questions.text: What is the primary limitation of self-assessment risk profiling tools?
options: Investors may guess socially desirable answers
questions.explanation: Investors may attempt to 'guess' the right answers instead of responding truthfully, reducing accuracy.

questions.text: Dynamic Asset Allocation uses:
options: Pre-defined models and valuation triggers for automatic rebalancing
questions.explanation: Dynamic asset allocation relies on pre-set models or valuation metrics to trigger portfolio rebalancing.

questions.text: Strategic Asset Allocation is based on:
options: Long-term goals and investor’s risk profile
questions.explanation: Strategic asset allocation aligns long-term goals, time horizon, and risk tolerance.

questions.text: Which personality trait is most associated with high risk-taking ability?
questions.explanation: Daring and adventurous individuals are psychologically more open to investment risks.

questions.text: Tactical Asset Allocation refers to:
options: Adjusting asset mix based on expected market behaviour
Maintaining static portfolios for long-term goals
questions.explanation: Tactical allocation uses market forecasts to temporarily change asset weights for potential gain.

questions.text: SEBI requires that a client’s risk profile must be:
options: Updated periodically or after major life changes
questions.explanation: Regulations mandate regular review, especially after life or financial changes, to ensure suitability.

questions.text: Strategic allocation is reviewed primarily when:
questions.explanation: Strategic allocation is long-term and revised mainly when fundamental changes occur in investor profile.

questions.text: Diversification works best when asset classes have:
questions.explanation: Low or negative correlation among asset classes ensures smoother portfolio performance.

questions.text: Which SEBI regulation mandates risk profiling by investment advisers?
questions.explanation: Regulation 16 of SEBI (Investment Advisers) Regulations, 2013 mandates risk profiling to ensure product suitability.

questions.text: Which of the following describes a conservative investor?
options: Prefers low risk and steady returns
Willing to take high risk for short-term gains
questions.explanation: Conservative investors prioritize capital protection and stable income over high returns.

questions.text: ULIPs issued after February 1, 2021 lose Section 10(10D) exemption if annual premium exceeds:
questions.explanation: ULIPs with premiums above ₹2.5 lakh per year no longer qualify for tax exemption under Section 10(10D).

questions.text: Category III Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs) require a minimum investment of:
questions.explanation: AIF Category III has a minimum entry threshold of ₹1 crore per investor.

questions.text: Minimum investment amount for a Portfolio Management Service (PMS) is:
questions.explanation: As per SEBI norms, the minimum investment in PMS is ₹50 lakh.

questions.text: What is the lock-in period for investments in PPF?
questions.explanation: PPF has a lock-in of 15 years, with partial withdrawals allowed after 5 years.

questions.text: Equity Linked Savings Scheme (ELSS) has a minimum lock-in period of:
questions.explanation: ELSS mutual funds have a 3-year lock-in, the shortest among tax-saving options under Section 80C.

questions.text: Which of the following offers exposure to infrastructure assets?
questions.explanation: Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) invest in infrastructure projects like roads, ports, and power plants.

questions.text: Sovereign Gold Bonds provide what annual interest rate?
questions.explanation: Sovereign Gold Bonds earn 2.5% interest per annum, paid semi-annually.

questions.text: Which of the following investment types carries the highest diversification benefit?
questions.explanation: Mutual funds pool investors’ money into diversified portfolios, reducing risk concentration.

questions.text: Mutual Funds are regulated by ______, while ULIPs are regulated by ______.
questions.explanation: Mutual funds fall under SEBI, while ULIPs are under the jurisdiction of IRDAI.

questions.text: Exchange Traded Funds (ETFs) differ from Index Funds because:
options: They are sold only by AMCs
They are traded on stock exchanges like shares
They are only available for debt instruments
questions.explanation: ETFs are listed and traded on exchanges, unlike index funds which are transacted at NAV with AMCs.

questions.text: Which of the following has the lowest cost of management?
questions.explanation: Index funds have the lowest expense ratios as they passively track a benchmark index.

questions.text: Which form of gold investment does NOT attract GST?
questions.explanation: Sovereign Gold Bonds are paper-based and exempt from GST.

questions.text: Which product among the following provides guaranteed returns?
questions.explanation: PPF offers government-backed guaranteed returns that vary quarterly with G-sec yields.

questions.case_text: Vivek has been investing in equity markets for the last 5 years. After a recent bull run, he believes he has developed a special ability to time the markets. He increases his trading frequency, ignores diversification and places large bets on a few stocks recommended by social media. He dismisses his earlier mistakes as ‘learning’.

questions.text: Vivek’s belief that he has special market-timing ability after recent success illustrates:
questions.explanation: Overconfidence bias leads investors to overestimate their skills and underestimate risks, especially after a period of success, encouraging excessive trading and concentrated positions.

questions.text: His tendency to ignore earlier mistakes and focus on recent gains reflects:
questions.explanation: Hindsight bias makes past events seem predictable, while recency bias causes recent performance to dominate memory, leading Vivek to overemphasize his latest success and downplay earlier losses.

questions.text: Concentrated bets on a few social-media-recommended stocks mainly increase which type of risk?
options: No risk, because tips are reliable
questions.explanation: Concentration and tip-based investing amplify stock-specific risk. Diversification helps reduce this unsystematic risk, which is under the investor’s control.

questions.text: From a behavioural finance standpoint, what should a financial planner do for Vivek?
options: Introduce goal-based investing and disciplined asset allocation with predefined rules
questions.explanation: Advisers must help clients transition from return-chasing and overconfidence toward a rules-based, goal-focused investment framework with appropriate diversification and risk control.

questions.text: Which of the following tools can help mitigate OVERCONFIDENCE?
options: Keeping a written investment policy and periodically reviewing results against benchmarks
questions.explanation: A written plan and objective performance review help investors realize the limitations of their predictions and reduce overconfident behaviour, promoting humility and discipline.

questions.case_text: Manoj (37) and Pooja (34) are a dual-income couple with one 4-year-old child. Manoj earns ₹1,20,000 per month and Pooja earns ₹80,000 per month. They have a home loan outstanding of ₹55 lakh with 18 years remaining and a car loan of ₹6 lakh. Their only life insurance is two traditional endowment policies: Manoj has ₹8 lakh sum assured and Pooja has ₹5 lakh sum assured. Both policies have been running for 6 years with moderate bonuses. Their adviser wants to evaluate whether they are adequately covered and whether they should restructure their life insurance to reduce risk and free up cash flow.

questions.text: Which is the MOST suitable method to estimate Manoj’s required life cover, considering his age, income and dependents?
options: Using only outstanding loan amounts as cover
Using Human Life Value (HLV) or income replacement method
Using only a fixed multiple of 2× annual income
Using maturity value of existing endowment plans
questions.explanation: The Human Life Value or income replacement method considers Manoj’s future income-earning potential, working years left, family’s lifestyle expenses and goals. This provides a comprehensive estimate of the capital required to replace his income on premature death, instead of simply matching loan amounts or using crude multiples.

questions.text: Why are Manoj’s and Pooja’s existing endowment policies likely to be INADEQUATE as sole life cover?
options: Endowment policies never pay on death
Endowment policies always lapse before maturity
Endowment policies provide relatively low risk cover for the premium paid
Endowment policies cannot be taken by salaried people
questions.explanation: Endowment policies combine savings and insurance, so for a given premium the sum assured is much lower than that of a pure term plan. With high income, loans and a young child, their required life cover will be a large multiple of ₹8 lakh and ₹5 lakh, making the current policies insufficient as the main protection tool.

questions.text: If Manoj decides to buy additional life cover, which product type is MOST appropriate to bridge the protection gap at minimum cost?
options: Pure term insurance with adequate sum assured
questions.explanation: A pure term policy provides large cover for low cost and is the most efficient way to close the mortality protection gap. Cash-value products like endowment or ULIP divert part of the premium to savings and therefore cannot provide the same level of protection per rupee of premium.

questions.text: Which of the following is a sensible way to treat the existing endowment policies if surrendering them results in a large loss and they still offer some bonus accrual?
options: Immediately surrender all policies regardless of loss
Continue them as paid-up and buy separate term cover for the gap
Buy no further life insurance at all
Assign the policy to the bank and stop paying premiums
questions.explanation: Making a policy paid-up reduces future premiums while preserving some benefits already built up. Manoj can then redirect freed-up cash flow to a term policy and investments, instead of continuing high premiums for low cover or incurring a heavy surrender loss.

questions.text: From a FAMILY RISK perspective, whose life should be insured for the larger sum assured?
options: Only Pooja’s life because she is younger
Primarily Manoj’s life as higher earner, and also Pooja’s life for her income contribution
Only joint life of both parents with very small cover
questions.explanation: Since Manoj’s income is higher, the impact of his death on the family’s finances would be greater. However, Pooja also contributes significantly, so both lives need adequate independent cover. The child’s life does not need life insurance because the child has no dependents.

questions.case_text: Mr. Mehta, 70, has two children. He owns a self-occupied house, some mutual fund investments and bank deposits. He has written a Will, leaving the house to his son and financial assets to his daughter. He wants to ensure that his estate passes smoothly to his heirs and is concerned about disputes and delays.

questions.text: Which document primarily governs distribution of Mr. Mehta’s assets after his death?
questions.explanation: A valid Will is the legal document expressing how his estate should be distributed after death, subject to laws of succession.

questions.text: What is one ADVANTAGE of REGISTERING a Will?
options: Registration provides additional evidentiary value and reduces risk of tampering
Registration exempts all assets from tax
questions.explanation: Registered Wills are kept with the registrar, reducing chances of loss or forgery and strengthening evidentiary value.

questions.text: If Mr. Mehta dies without leaving a valid Will, the succession will be governed by:
questions.explanation: In absence of a Will, the estate devolves as per personal laws (Hindu Succession Act, etc.) relating to intestate succession.

questions.text: Which person is responsible for administering the estate as per the Will?
questions.explanation: The testator appoints an executor in the Will to carry out its instructions and distribute assets accordingly.

questions.text: To reduce the risk of disputes, Mr. Mehta should:
options: Keep his Will completely secret without clarity
Clearly communicate intentions to family and ensure Will is unambiguous
questions.explanation: Clear drafting, unambiguous bequests and open communication often reduce misunderstandings and legal disputes.

questions.case_text: Meera, 58, is nearing retirement. She has built a corpus of ₹1.5 crore and expects her monthly post-retirement expenses initially to be ₹80,000. She expects inflation at 5% p.a. and believes her post-retirement portfolio can earn 7% p.a. She wants a withdrawal strategy that minimizes the risk of her corpus running out.

questions.text: What is the approximate REAL return she can expect post-retirement?
questions.explanation: Real return ≈ (1.07 / 1.05 – 1) ≈ 1.9%, which is close to 2%.

questions.text: Which withdrawal approach is generally considered safer for long retirement periods?
options: A sustainable percentage of corpus with periodic review
Withdrawing only interest every year irrespective of inflation
questions.explanation: A disciplined, sustainable withdrawal rate (like 3–4% real) with periodic review helps reduce the risk of depleting the corpus.

questions.text: If Meera invests entirely in a fixed deposit earning 7% and inflation is 5%, what is the long-term risk?
options: Her real purchasing power may erode over time
Corpus will double every 3 years in real terms
questions.explanation: Even though nominal value may grow, inflation-adjusted purchasing power increases only marginally and may turn negative if expenses grow faster.

questions.text: Which of the following instruments can provide a GUARANTEED lifelong income stream?
questions.explanation: Immediate annuities convert a lump sum into a periodic income stream, guaranteeing payments as per chosen option.

questions.text: Which portfolio approach is MOST suitable for Meera’s retirement years?
options: Balanced mix of debt and some equity
questions.explanation: A balanced allocation ensures stability through debt while equity portion helps combat inflation over a long retirement horizon.

questions.case_text: A retiree, Mrs. D’Souza, is offered two investment choices by her adviser: (A) A product that ‘guarantees’ she will not lose money, but with low return; (B) A balanced fund that may fluctuate but has better long-term return prospects. She chooses the guaranteed option because she fears any possibility of loss.

questions.text: Mrs. D’Souza’s preference for avoiding losses even at the cost of lower returns is an example of:
questions.explanation: Loss aversion is the tendency to prefer avoiding losses more strongly than acquiring equivalent gains.

questions.text: Her adviser presents option A emphasizing ‘no loss’ and option B emphasizing ‘possible loss’, which is an example of:
questions.explanation: How choices are framed (in terms of gains or losses) can influence decisions even when underlying outcomes are similar.

questions.text: What is the RISK of her choice if inflation is higher than her guaranteed return?
options: Erosion of real purchasing power over time
questions.explanation: If nominal returns are below inflation, her real wealth and purchasing power will decline gradually.

questions.text: Which approach better balances her fear and need for growth?
options: Mix of guaranteed products with some exposure to balanced funds
questions.explanation: A combination ensures she has a safe base while some assets aim to protect against inflation over the long term.

questions.text: What is an adviser’s responsibility in this situation?
options: Explain trade-offs between safety and growth in simple terms
questions.explanation: Advisers must help clients understand both the comfort and long-term consequences of their risk choices.

questions.case_text: Sanjay, 45, works in a manufacturing unit. His employer provides a group personal accident cover of ₹10 lakh. He is considering whether to buy additional personal accident insurance for himself and his homemaker spouse and wants to understand how accident insurance differs from life insurance.

questions.text: What does a PERSONAL ACCIDENT policy primarily cover?
options: Death or disability due to accident only
questions.explanation: Personal accident policies protect against death, permanent or partial disablement caused by accidental events, not all causes of death.

questions.text: Which risk is NOT covered by a pure accident policy?
options: Permanent total disability due to road accident
Death due to illness such as heart attack
Loss of limbs due to accident
questions.explanation: Accident policies do not cover death due to natural causes or illness; these are covered by life or health insurance.

questions.text: Why might Sanjay still need LIFE INSURANCE even if he has accident insurance?
options: Life insurance covers death from illness and other causes
questions.explanation: Life insurance covers death from any cause (as per policy terms), including illness, which accident policies do not cover.

questions.text: Is it appropriate to buy personal accident cover for Sanjay’s homemaker spouse?
options: Yes, because an accident can cause loss of her valuable unpaid work
Only if she has a salary
questions.explanation: Accident cover for a homemaker can help defray medical costs and the cost of replacing her services in the household if she is disabled.

questions.text: Which combination MOST appropriately covers Sanjay’s family risks?
options: Term life insurance plus adequate health and accident cover
Only group life insurance from employer
questions.explanation: A holistic risk management framework includes term life cover, health insurance, and personal accident cover tailored to family needs.
